title: The 10 Small Asks Swipe File: Cold Email CTAs That Get More Replies
description: An 85M-email report found meeting asks cut replies 44% and offers lifted them 28%. Copy 10 small asks, plus the 4-step offer play.
lead: This is the full 10 small asks swipe file from the reel. Asking a stranger for a 30-minute meeting is a big ask. This guide gives you 10 small asks to copy, the data behind them, and the 4-step play that turns a one-word "yes" into a booked call.
insider: Small asks are how we end client emails: one easy question, then the call comes after the yes. In our small pilot, **10,284 people contacted turned into 417 replies and 103 sales opportunities**, about 1 in every 100 people. Writing one good ask is easy. Testing asks across thousands of emails, every day, is what we do for clients.

blocks.text: Why "Can we hop on a call?" fails
A meeting request asks a stranger for half an hour of their day, before they even know if you can help. Most people say nothing. Silence is easier than no.

The data agrees. In [The Ultimate Cold Email Data Report](https://tactics.30mpc.com/hubfs/The%20Ultimate%20Cold%20Email%20Data%20Report-1.pdf) by Gong, 30 Minutes to President's Club and Jason Bay (85M+ cold emails), **asking for a meeting cut reply rates by 44%**, and **making an offer lifted reply rates by 28%**. The report's advice: ask for interest, or make an offer like a free trial, a data report or an audit.
**Why small asks work:** "Worth a look?" can be answered with one word. The reader doesn't have to check their calendar or commit to anything. They only have to say yes to learning more.
The 10 small asks

head: The ask
Use it when
rows: The default. Use it after any short, clear email.
"Can I send the playbook we used for a firm like yours?"
You have a real process you can share.
"Want me to send the exact campaign we ran for a [industry] company?"
You have a real result in their industry.
"Open to a 2-minute video showing how this would work for [company]?"
Your offer is easier to show than to explain.
You have real data or a case study with results.
"Want a free [audit / teardown] of your [site / emails / ads]? No call needed."
You can give real value in under an hour of work.
"Is this on your list this quarter, or later?"
You want to know timing without pushing.
"Are you the right person for this, or is it someone else on your team?"
You're not sure who owns the problem.
"Want me to send a short checklist for [problem]?"
You're early and have no case studies yet.
"If this isn't a priority, just reply 'no' and I'll leave it there."
Last email in a sequence. Makes saying no easy.

blocks.label: Swipe file: all 10 asks
blocks.text:
1. Worth a look?
2. Can I send the playbook we used for a firm like yours?
3. Want me to send the exact campaign we ran for a [industry] company?
4. Open to a 2-minute video showing how this would work for [company]?
5. Should I send over the numbers?
6. Want a free [audit / teardown] of your [site / emails / ads]? No call needed.
7. Is this on your list this quarter, or later?
8. Are you the right person for this, or is it someone else on your team?
9. Want me to send a short checklist for [problem]?
10. If this isn't a priority, just reply 'no' and I'll leave it there.

blocks.label: Pick one
blocks.text: Use only one ask per email. Two asks means the reader has to choose, and choosing is work.
The 4-step offer play
Step 1: Offer something first
Can I send the playbook we used for a firm like yours?
**Why:** you give before you take. The reader gets something useful even if they never buy. That's what makes the offer easy to say yes to.
Step 2: Wait for the yes

Don't attach the playbook to the first email. Don't add a link. Let them reply "sure" or "yes, send it". **A reply is the goal of the first email.** It also means they asked for what you send next, so it isn't cold anymore.
Step 3: Send it, then offer one time to walk through it
Send what you promised, right away. Then offer one specific time, not a calendar link with 40 slots. One time is a simple yes or no.

blocks.label: After-the-yes message
blocks.text:
Hi [first name],

Here it is: [link or attachment].

The part most [role]s find useful is [section or page], where [one-line summary].

Happy to walk you through how it would work for [company]. Does [day] at [time] work for 15 minutes?

[your name]
Step 4: Make it worth a look

The ask only works if the thing you offer is actually worth having. A "free consultation" is a sales call with a nicer name, and everyone knows it. The exact campaign you ran for a firm like theirs is real value.

head: Weak offer
Strong offer
rows: The exact campaign we ran for a firm like yours
A 2-minute video of it working on your website
The playbook, with the real numbers
A free audit of your [emails / ads / site], no call needed

Why it hurts
Fix

blocks.text: Write your small ask with Claude

blocks.label: Small ask prompt
blocks.text:
Here is my cold email:
[paste email]

What I can really offer for free (only things I have ready): [playbook / case study / audit / checklist / video]
My real results I can share: [facts, or "none yet"]

1. Find the ask at the end of my email and tell me if it's a meeting ask.
2. Write 5 new endings. Each one must be a small ask the reader can answer in one or two words, like "Worth a look?".
3. At least 2 of them must offer one of my free things.
4. Don't invent results, don't add links, don't mention a call or meeting length.

blocks.label: The rule
blocks.text: Ask for a word, not half an hour. The call comes after the yes.

resources.note: What to say when they answer "not now"

faq.q: When should I ask for the meeting?
faq.a: After the yes. Once they've said "sure, send it", send what you promised and offer one specific time to walk them through it.

faq.q: What if I don't have a playbook or case study yet?
faq.a: Offer something small you can make in an hour: a checklist, 3 ideas for their company, or a short audit. Never offer something you don't have.

faq.q: Does "Worth a look?" work in every industry?
faq.a: It's a good start almost everywhere because it's so easy to answer. Test it against one offer-style ask and keep the one that gets more replies.

faq.q: Can I use more than one ask in a sequence?
faq.a: Yes. Use a different small ask in each follow-up. Just keep one ask per email.
